  59: must take into account the space-distributed aspect of railway
  60: infrastructure. Railway assets are often not spatially delimited to
  61: a certain point, which implies difﬁculties in the organization of
  62: maintenance activities and resources. Another aspect that makes
  63: railway maintenance critical is the time constraint. In fact, the
  64: available time for maintenance is very limited due to various
  65: factors, such as railroad trafﬁc, climate, and interrelations among
  66: different maintenance projects. Some of these requirements
  67: result in soft constraints, i.e., violations that can be tolerated
  68: if no better choices exist, while others are hard constraints that
  69: can never be violated.
  70: To cope with this problem, many maintenance approaches
  71: have been developed in the relevant literature. Among these are:
  72: 1) planned maintenance, performed on a regular, ﬁxed time
  73: schedule. It can lead to a signiﬁcant reduction in the
  74: useful life of components due to early replacement and
  75: unnecessary ap r i o r ischeduled maintenance activities;
  76: 2) condition-based maintenance, performed only when nec-
  77: essary, on the basis of the continuously monitored asset
  78: conditions. This approach allows for better usage of in-
  79: frastructure components but requires regular and frequent
  80: monitoring of the degradation state of railway assets;
  81: 3) predictive maintenance, performed only when necessary,
  82: on the basis of suitable model estimations.
  83: The last approach, which is considered in the present work,
  84: guarantees the greatest reduction in maintenance costs, since
  85: maintenance is performed only when necessary, with a limited
  86: number of monitoring measures required. To this end, the aim of
  87: predictive railway maintenance is minimizing the probability of
  88: the occurrence during train service of so-called mission-critical
  89: faults, i.e., those that prevent trains from circulating, leading
  90: to service disruptions, while keeping maintenance costs as low
  91: as possible. Nevertheless, the planning of rail maintenance is
  92: still based on long-term planned maintenance strategies, with
  93: static decisions manually deﬁned by the human operator and
  94: rediscussed only in case of critical events, without automatic
  95: support.
  96: This article is aimed at addressing the abovementioned situa-
  97: tion, supporting maintenance decision-makers in case of the oc-
  98: currence of unexpected events, taking into account, in quasi-real
  99: time, information and data from the ﬁeld. This work represents
 100: the extension of previous research on the ofﬂine scheduling of

 109: 2 IEEE TRANSACTIONS ON RELIABILITY
 110: study was aimed at developing a model to plan interventions
 111: on the technological assets of a rail network when they reach
 112: a certain degradation state, the present study introduces the
 113: management of uncertainty in maintenance planning and deals
 114: with a different application. In particular, the focus of this article
 115: is on determining the maintenance deadlines for a maintenance
 116: scheduling problem by means of a predictive model of rail
 117: vertical deformation, characterized by spatial discretization and
 118: uncertainties.
 119: The whole approach is based on the risk minimization frame-
 120: work, according to ISO 55 000 guidelines [2], and introduces
 121: the concept of risk in railway maintenance activities’ scheduling.
 122: This implies that maintenance activities’ priorities are based on
 123: certain criticality indexes that take into account both the prob-
 124: ability of a failure event and the relevant losses. A degradation
 125: model is proposed to evaluate the probability of rail track failure.
 126: In addition, the proposed approach allows for the dynamic
 127: adaptation of maintenance schedules in reaction to the occur-
 128: rence of unexpected events that characterize real environments,
 129: such as unpredicted signiﬁcant degradations. To deal with this
 130: aspect, an online recovery methodology based on a rolling-
 131: horizon (RH) approach, aiming at scheduling fault diagnosis
 132: and fault management activities, is considered.
 133: The main innovative aspects are the possibility of shifting
 134: from the corrective and planned maintenance strategies that are
 135: currently in use to predictive maintenance strategies for rail
 136: track, and from manual procedures based on operators judgment
 137: to an automated decision process based on the data analysis and
 138: optimization algorithms.
 139: This article describes how the presented approach allows for
 140: 1) early/timely identiﬁcation and correction of critical de-
 141: fects and the mitigation of the risk of service disruptions;
 142: 2) optimization of maintenance plans based on the correct
 143: estimation of current and future infrastructure conditions;
 144: 3) efﬁcient exploitation of track access times (maximiza-
 145: tion of the number of activities executed in the available
 146: time frame, reduction of the time needed to complete the
 147: planned maintenance activities);
 148: 4) a high level of ﬂexibility in the maintenance process,
 149: including in cases of unexpected events, fostering service
 150: resiliency.
 151: The article is organized as follows. In Section II, the existing
 152: literature on maintenance scheduling and recovery models is
 153: analyzed. In Section III-V, the stochastic degradation model
 154: and the mathematical formulation of the planning problem are
 155: presented. Finally, an application of the proposed approach to
 156: a Swedish rail line, the results and some indications on future
 157: developments are discussed.
 158: II. L ITERA TUREREVIEW
 159: Preventive maintenance works are carried out to reduce
 160: the probability of the occurrence of failures and to improve
 161: the overall reliability and availability of a system. Poorly de-
 162: signed preventive maintenance schedules may incur high main-
 163: tenance and operational costs and loss of safety. Therefore,
 164: the literature paid great attention to railway maintenance
 165: scheduling problems. Many researchers agreed on the need to
 166: move from planned preventive maintenance to predictive pre-
 167: ventive maintenance [3]. In the rail sector, automatic monitoring
 168: and diagnostic systems, both mounted aboard trains and track-
 169: side, have become increasingly signiﬁcant and sophisticated,
 170: and suitable models are necessary to efﬁciently use the newly
 171: available data to estimate when a fault is likely to occur and
 172: adapt maintenance interventions accordingly [4]. Scheduling
 173: models for predictive maintenance must be able to reduce both
 174: the overall maintenance budget and the safety risk, evaluating
 175: the priority of maintenance tasks, taking into account not only
 176: assets’ degradation conditions but also asset criticalities. One
 177: fault may be better tolerated by the system than another, based
 178: on the related consequences. In previous literature, the most
 179: common optimization criteria for railway maintenance were
 180: based on cost minimization to reduce the overall maintenance
 181: budget. Today, the aim of predictive maintenance scheduling
 182: is to minimize both the time duration and overall costs of
 183: maintenance, to plan maintenance activities by assigning them to
 184: the available teams, and to maximize the system’s reliability and
 185: availability at the same time [5]–[7]. More speciﬁcally, mathe-
 186: matical models were developed to determine the assignment and
 187: schedules of maintenance teams to minimize the disruption of
 188: train operations and the infrastructure possession time [8]–[11].
 189: Such models take into account budget constraints, train sched-
 190: ules, maintenance teams’ travel times, and various interrelations
 191: among maintenance activities. The solutions consist of heuristic
 192: approaches such as the tabu search approach and the simpler
 193: greedy heuristic. Nevertheless, they do not take into account
 194: data on the infrastructure conditions provided by monitoring
 195: systems. Some steps forward in this direction were described
 196: in [12]–[16]. In fact, these models aim to minimize the proba-
 197: bility of mission-critical faults during train service, keeping the
 198: railway track at good safety and comfort levels. The used data
 199: from special diagnostic trains and new inspection technologies
 200: to evaluate current track conditions. The increased availability of
 201: data allow for the development of a data-driven strategy to assess
 202: infrastructure conditions [17]–[19]. On the other hand, [20]–
 203: [23] developed tools based on predictive degradation models,
 204: providing important steps from condition-based maintenance
 205: toward predictive maintenance. In these approaches, track con-
 206: dition data allow for prediction of faults and determination of
 207: which maintenance work is required for safe train operation and
 208: whether safety-related speed restrictions are necessary. These
 209: models enable long-term forecasts of rail conditions [24] and
 210: strategic maintenance decisions that also consider the uncer-
 211: tainties of the deterioration process, but they do not consider
 212: asset criticalities. In other works [25]–[27], reliability concepts
 213: were applied to plan periodic maintenance while also taking
 214: into account asset criticalities by means of failure mode effect
 215: and criticality analysis or Bayesian network procedures. These
 216: approaches incorporate risk-based methodologies to estimate
 217: the optimal time of replacement or repair of a railway structure,
 218: but they do not take into account a predictive model of asset
 219: conditions.

 225: CONSILVIO et al.: RH APPROACH FOR PREDICTIVE MAINTENANCE PLANNING TO REDUCE THE RISK 3
 226: Therefore, in the literature, many different approaches to the
 227: scheduling of maintenance activities were proposed; neverthe-
 228: less, new steps forward are needed to adapt railway maintenance
 229: scheduling to both predictive models’ inputs and risk-based
 230: asset management standards [28]. In this context, the present
 231: study aims to provide a systemic view of how scheduling
 232: models can use the signiﬁcant outputs of predictive tools and
 233: degradation models based on railway ﬁeld data to achieve a
 234: risk-based maintenance plan that can be adapted according
 235: to updated inputs. As mentioned, in real environments, pre-
 236: dictive maintenance scheduling must address the occurrence
 237: of unexpected events due to the intrinsically stochastic nature
 238: of the system. The problems of uncertainty in the scheduling
 239: process and the discrepancy between theoretical schedules and
 240: real system behavior were faced in the literature evaluating the
 241: risk associated with the occurrence of unfavorable events, such
 242: as machine unavailability or delays [29], [30]. Other studies
 243: considered dynamic rescheduling to achieve fault recovery in
 244: real-time systems [31], [32]. Regarding maintenance schedul-
 245: ing, Ma et al. [33] dealt with the fact that a maintenance schedule
 246: is enacted based on a statistical average. This still presents the
 247: unavoidable risk that the system might fail before the criteria
 248: are exceeded: a failure might occur unexpectedly. Nevertheless,
 249: in the railway ﬁeld, rescheduling research was mostly applied
 250: to train disruptions for the management of rail trafﬁc in case of
 251: delays or unexpected events [34], [35]. Other works considered
 252: the problem of train rescheduling under uncertainties due to
 253: infrastructure maintenance [36], [37]. Some steps towards the
 254: management of uncertainty in rail maintenance were made by
 255: Osman et al. [38], who identiﬁed potential sources of disruption
 256: to predetermined track inspection schedules, such as loss of
 257: crews, machine breakdowns, and special inspection requests,
 258: and by Su et al. [39], who presented a multilevel planning
 259: model for railway maintenance, highlighting the uncertainty
 260: at different planning levels and proposing a scenario-based
 261: approach to dealing with it. Nevertheless, these studies focused
 262: on a condition-based maintenance strategy, presenting a cyclical
 263: approach to updating inspection schedules. The present work
 264: introduces uncertainty management within a predictive main-
 265: tenance framework, reducing the computational effort of the
 266: stochastic programming model described in [40], which deals
 267: with rail track maintenance by introducing a large number of
 268: constraints associated with samples of the random variables
 269: representing the uncertain deadlines derived from predictive
 270: models.

 277: model, developed by means of data collected by measurement
 278: cars from 2011 to 2016 on a single track line in Sweden,
 279: provides the rail deformation over time of the given rail stretches.

 466: IV . ROLLING-HORIZON FRAMEWORK
 467: In this article, a RH approach is considered
 468: r to introduce certain dynamics into maintenance planning;
 469: r to reduce the computational effort.
 470: With reference to the ﬁrst bullet point, the RH framework
 471: allows to reconsider, in any time window, non-executed activ-
 472: ities from the previous window, due, for example, to delays,
 473: and to introduce new assets whose degradation has reached a
 474: nonforecast unacceptable degradation state.
 475: With respect to the second bullet, scheduling the mainte-
 476: nance activities for all the rail stretches in R may result in a
 477: very difﬁcult task due to the huge computational complexity
 478: of scheduling, which is well known to be a non-deterministic
 479: polynomial-time NP-hard problem. Therefore, within the RH
 480: framework, the set of rail stretches considered at any generic
 481: instant th is signiﬁcantly reduced to the subset A = {i ∈R :
 482: th ≤ τi
 483: R < Δt} of the rail stretches that will require mainte-
 484: nance activities within a certain, ap r i o r i–deﬁned horizon Δt.
 485: As a consequence, the maintenance planning of the complete
 486: set R of rail stretches can be divided into a set of repeatedly
 487: solved sub-problems. In this vein, if the time needed for the
 488: problem solution is Tmax, the optimization problem is stated
 489: in th −Tmax. This parameter can be chosen according to the
 490: available computational resources for the problem solution.
 491: In addition, in the proposed RH approach, the solution is
 492: applied only to the maintenance activities with a completion
 493: Fig. 4. Example of the rolling-horizon framework. Dark colors indicate
 494: scheduled and executed maintenance activities; light colors represent scheduled
 495: activities to be reconsidered in the next optimization problem.
 496: time within the interval 2 [th,th +δt[, where δt is a parameter
 497: that deﬁnes the time interval of the ﬁxed maintenance plan.
 498: This choice has the advantage of allowing for planning of the
 499: activities in the hth RH frame while taking into account at least
 500: part of the activities that will be considered in the (h+1) th
 501: frame, thus leaving a certain degree of freedom for the latter
 502: activities, which can, then, be rediscussed. Therefore, while
 503: a maintenance plan of length δt is actually applied, a rolling
 504: horizonΔt>δ t is planned with the aims of:
 505: 1) possibly bringing forward some activities into frame h
 506: if other required maintenance activities are ﬁnished in
 507: advance;
 508: 2) possibly postponing some activities to the next frame h+
 509: 1 to execute activities on assets located in nearby positions;
 510: 3) optimizing the scheduling of the nonexecuted activities of
 511: frameh due to unexpected failures or updated information
 512: on asset status within the plan of frame h+1 .
 513: High values of Δt imply high ﬂexibility, in particular with
 514: reference to 1) and 2), but also a high computational effort, due
 515: to the larger dimension of the sub-problem instances. The choice
 516: of the parametersΔt andδt depends on the allowed operational
 517: ﬂexibility since it implies how often a solution can be rediscussed
 518: and the updated plan provided to maintenance operators. In the
 519: performed experiments, a value Δt ≈ 1.5δt has been proven to
 520: be a good compromise.
 521: An example of two generic subsequent RH frames is reported
 522: in Fig. 4, where the maintenance activities of rail stretches 3 and
 523: 6 are planned in the interval [th +δt,th +Δt[ and then consid-
 524: ered in the next frame, when they are scheduled and executed.
 525: Analogously, the maintenance activities of rail stretches 8 and
 526: 10 are scheduled but not executed in the (h+1) th RH frame.

 561: A. Assumptions
 562: In the formulation of the MILP problem, the following as-
 563: sumptions have been considered to model real-world operational
 564: aspects.
 565: 1) Any interval [th,th +Δt[, h =0 ,1,... , can be divided
 566: into (discontinuous) train-free subintervals, gathered in
 567: the set T , during which train circulation is forbidden and
 568: maintenance activities can be performed.
 569: 2) Preemption of maintenance activities is not allowed.
 570: 3) All maintenance teams are available at the initial time.
 571: 4) All maintenance teams are unrelated, and each mainte-
 572: nance activity can be processed by any free team.
 573: 5) To allow for normal circulation outside train-free intervals,
 574: the tamping machines must be able to reach the nearest
 575: parking rail at the end of the last maintenance activity
 576: in each train-free interval. Fig. 6 shows the assignment
 577: of the parking slots to the different segments of the rail
 578: line. Therefore, the setup time is different depending on
 579: whether the consecutive activities on the rail stretchesi and
 580: j are executed in the same interval r or not. In particular,
 581: the setup time is composed of the travel time from the
 582: location of the rail stretch i to the location of rail stretch
 583: j if they are maintained in the same interval; on the other
 584: hand, if the activity ofj is performed in the intervalr +1 ,
 585: the setup time consists of the travel time from the tamping
 586: machine parking slot i⋆nearest to i (usually consisting of
 587: a secondary rail in a station).
 588: These assumptions are representative of the considered main-
 589: tenance process consisting of tamping activities along a rail line.
 590: Nevertheless, Assumptions 3 and 4 can be easily removed by
 591: modifying the related problem constraints.
 592: B. MILP F ormulation
 593: This section introduces and describes the optimization prob-
 594: lem for the maintenance of a set of assets distributed along
 595: a railway line. Thanks to the previously described translation
 596: scheme, the proposed formulation is valid for all frames h ∈H .
 597: The problem structure refers to the single-line version proposed
 598: in [1] since the focus of the present work is on the dynamics of
 599: railway maintenance. A single instance of the problem is recon-
 600: sidered in each time slot h ∈H making up the RH framework.
 601: However, the problem in [1] can be used in place of the one
 602: described in this section to easily switch to the network problem.
 603: In addition, a new characteristic of the present problem consists
 604: of the introduction of a particular constraint aimed at taking
 605: into account the time needed by the tamping machine to reach
 606: a parking slot. Before the problem is described, two dummy
 607: activities i =0 and j = |A|+1 are artiﬁcially introduced to
 608: correctly identify the ﬁrst and last real activities.

 782: The weights λc and λq in (7) are chosen by the maintenance
 783: service provider in line with the strategic goals of its organization
 784: (more importance attributed to minimization of the completion
 785: time or to minimization of tardiness with respect to the soft

 790: of the soft deadlines negligible in the cost function, the assets
 791: remain in an acceptably degraded condition. Moreover, the
 792: obtained experimental results are quite insensitive to the weights
 793: λc andλq , as a variation of the cost function of 10% was obtained
 794: by varying the weights by 50%.
 795: C. Problem Solution
 796: The problem deﬁned by (6)–(21) is NP-hard; therefore, it is
 797: characterized by a very high computational effort and requires
 798: the deﬁnition of effective heuristic strategies to be solved. In this
 799: article, a MATHeuristic approach is considered.
 800: The development of the solution algorithm is outside the scope
 801: of this article; nevertheless, some information is provided. The
 802: algorithm is based on an iterative approach, which provides new
 803: solutions by performing successive optimizations of a reduced
 804: subset of randomly chosen variables. The considered algorithm
 805: is reported in Algorithm 1, while the relevant notation is de-
 806: ﬁned in Table III. The advantage of the hybrid MATHeuristic
 807: approach is the possibility of combining the strength of exact
 808: methods with the ﬂexibility of an approximated metaheuristic.
 809: This methodology has been proven to be a very competitive alter-
 810: native to solving large-scale instances of complex optimization
 811: problems [47]. The algorithm starts from an initial admissible
 812: top-to-end solution, consisting of executing the activities on
 813: the assets as sorted along the line while assigning the ﬁrst
 814: |A|/2 activities to the ﬁrst team and the remaining ones to
 815: the second team. The choice of the top-to-end initial solution
 816: is due not only to its simplicity but also to the fact that such
 817: TABLE III
 818: NOTATION OF ALGORITHM 1
 819: Fig. 7. Cost function values over 8 RH frames for the case study described in
 820: Section VI.
 821: a strategy is often applied in the real-world maintenance of
 822: geographically distributed assets. Regarding the performance
 823: of the MATHeuristic technique, the applications of the proposed
 824: approach to the considered case study yield average reductions
 825: of approximately 45% of the cost function with respect to the
 826: reference top-to-end solution.
 827: As reported in Algorithm 1, at the end of each iteration, if
 828: the whole solution improves, the new values of the optimized
 829: variables are accepted; otherwise, they are dropped. Actually,
 830: the solution never worsens, as ˜Yu ∪Yfix is always a feasible
 831: solution; nevertheless, if˜Yu,⋆= ˜Yu, the whole solution does not
 832: improve, as shown in Fig. 7, where the ﬂat shapes indicate that
 833: there are no improvements. The iterative approach is applied
 834: for Tmax hours. As the solution never worsens within an RH
 835: window, the peaks in Fig. 7 represent the transition between RH
 836: frames: since new maintenance activities are considered, the
 837: cost function may be much greater than the optimal value of the
 838: previous period. Finally, since the ﬁnal solution of one RH frame
 839: represents the initial solution for the next one, this initial solution
 840: may be infeasible. This infeasibility is simply overcome by the
 841: MATHeuristic approach by varying the subset of considered
 842: variables. In particular, in the new RH window, if the previous
 843: solution is infeasible, the ﬁrst iterations of theMATHeuristic will
 844: ﬁnd a feasible initial solution for that RH window, while the
 845: successive iterations will optimize the feasible initial solution
 846: by randomly choosing a subset of variables. Therefore, the

 881: D. Solution Example
 882: In this section, an example is reported with the aim of ex-
 883: plaining the RH approach in detail. In this regard, for the sake of
 884: clarity, it is assumed that t1 =0 ,δt =1 days and Δt =4 days.
 885: Then, let|A| = {1,3,8,10,12,19,23,26,29,30} be the subset
 886: of rail stretches that need to be considered in the maintenance
 887: plan.
 888: Example 1. Delay of an Activity: In this example, during the

 946: VI. C ASE STUDY
 947: In this section, a case study is presented with the aim of
 948: showing the average performance of the proposed approach in a
 949: real-world scenario. To this end, the considered application con-
 950: sists of dynamic planning of tamping maintenance activities on
 951: a single-track line in Sweden managed by the Swedish Transport
 952: Administration (Traﬁkverket). As mentioned, the considered
 953: rail track is basically a freight line, although some passenger
 954: trains also use the line. The annual trafﬁc volume is between 20
 955: million gross tons (MGTs) and 27 MGTs. The train speed on the
 956: line is in the 80–120 km/h category. The line is composed of a
 957: continuous welded rail of the head-hardened 60E1 rail type, with
 958: concrete sleepers and Pandrol e-clip fasteners. The maximum
 959: allowable axle load on the line section is 30 t. The considered
 960: railway stretch of 200 km is divided into 200 equal segments
 961: of 1 km each. The maintenance activities can be scheduled
 962: only during train-free intervals, that is, from 0 A.M.t o5 A.M.
 963: Hence, a working day consists of ﬁve hours during which the
 964: teams move along the line and perform the activities (tamping
 965: machines can move only when there are no circulating trains).
 966: Two maintenance teams M1 and M2, equipped with the same
 967: single-sleeper tamping machine, are available for maintenance,
 968: each starting its ﬁrst travel from the depot. Before the end
 969: of each train-free interval, each maintenance team reaches the
 970: nearest parking slot. The travel time from the nearest parking
 971: slot (usually consisting of a secondary rail in a station) to the
 972: location of the next asset i is considered at the beginning of the
 973: next train-free interval, as deﬁned in (11) and in Assumption 5 in
 974: Section V. Eight parking slots are considered at kilometers 25,
 975: 50, 75, 100, 125, 150, 175, and 200.
 976: Regarding the maintenance performance, the teams’ working
 977: speed is set to 500 m of tamped rail per hour, and the traveling
 978: speed between two rail stretches that have to be maintained is
 979: set to 40 km/h.
 980: As mentioned, the considered degradation model is provided
 981: by Famurewa et al. in [41], [42] and was developed by analyzing
 982: the geometry data collected by measurement cars from 2011 to
 983: 2016 in the considered Swedish single-track line. Nevertheless,
 984: for conﬁdentiality reasons, realistic realizations are considered
 985: in each RH frame by randomly extracting the values of the
 986: initial deformationδi(τi
 987: k) and of the coefﬁcientαi from uniform
 988: distributions with upper and lower boundaries as deﬁned in
 989: Famurewa et al. [41], [42]. For the same reason, the variance
 990: value of the error ϵis set to σ2 =0 .15 mm2.
 991: Concerning the deadlines and the release time, in the present
 992: case study, they refer to the European Standards [43] and the
 993: Swedish National Railway Regulation [46], which identify the
 994: safety-related limits for each track geometry parameter, provid-
 995: ing limits for different categories of severity:
 996: 1) an alert limit (AL) is deﬁned as the limit that, if ex-
 997: ceeded, triggers the track geometry consideration in reg-
 998: ularly planned maintenance operations. This threshold
 999: customizes the deﬁnition of the release time provided
1000: in Section III, which is deﬁned as the instant at which
1001: the probability of reaching the AL exceeds the value
1002: pR =1 0−8 (equivalent toγR =1 0−3);
1003: 2) an intervention limit (IL) refers to the value that, if ex-
1004: ceeded, indicates corrective maintenance must be per-
1005: formed to prevent the immediate action limit from being
1006: reached. This threshold deﬁnes the hard and soft deadlines
1007: that correspond to the abovementioned deﬁned threshold
1008: ¯δ. In this regard, the hard and soft deadlines are deﬁned as
1009: the instants at which the probability of reaching the IL ex-
1010: ceeds the values ofpH =1 0−5 andpS =1 0−7 (equivalent
1011: to γS =1 0−2), respectively;
1012: 3) an immediate action limit refers to the value that, if ex-
1013: ceeded, requires the imposition of immediate measures,
1014: such as closing the line or reducing the speed, to reduce
1015: the risk to an acceptable level. This threshold should never
1016: be reached by rail deformation and is not considered in the
1017: present work.
1018: Regarding the choice of the probabilitiespR,pH , andpS , their
1019: values are set in analogy to the safety integrity level standard and
1020: in particular the SIL1 failure probability, which is 10−5.
1021: The alert and intervention limits are provided by [46] and are
1022: 16 mm and 19 mm, respectively.
1023: To set up the experiments, it is also considered that:
1024: 1) activity delays are randomly generated in the simulated
1025: scenario, considering a probability of 10−2;
1026: 2) the priority of each rail stretch is initially set to 1, and it
1027: doubles if the activity is not executed in the planned RH
1028: frame and must be reconsidered;
1029: 3) unpredicted maintenance activities are randomly intro-
1030: duced with the occurrence rate of 10−2 per RH frame.
1031: A. Results
1032: The monthly maintenance plan is evaluated considering a
1033: rolling window of one week and setting δt =7 days, Δt =1 0
1034: days, and Tmax =1 h.

1043: Regarding the algorithm performance, consider the cost func-
1044: tion values computed for each iteration of the MATHeuristic
1045: algorithm and for all the RH frames depicted in Fig. 7. In that
1046: ﬁgure, each peak represents the transition between two con-
1047: secutive RH frames, (th,th +Δt) and (t(h+1),t (h+1) +Δt).
1048: Therefore, due to the newly introduced maintenance activities
1049: to be scheduled and to the updated problem parameters, the
1050: ﬁrst value of the cost function in each window is much greater
1051: than the optimal value computed in the previous window. As
1052: mentioned in Section V -C, the performance of theMATHeuristic
1053: approach is compared with the basic top-to-end solution and
1054: results in an average reduction of 45% of the relevant cost
1055: function values. As mentioned, this basic top-to-end solution
1056: is considered only in the ﬁrst RH window, as also indicated in
1057: Fig. 7, while the initial solution in the next window is the best
1058: solution from the previous window.
1059: The results of the application of the RH approach to the
1060: considered scenario are reported in Table IV, where the average
1061: values of the main parameters, computed over 30 runs of the
1062: proposed RH model, are indicated.
1063: More speciﬁcally, the results show that the approach allows
1064: for the planning of maintenance interventions while dealing with
1065: the stochastic aspect of the rail deformation process, guarantee-
1066: ing a failure probability of7.5×10−6, lower than the maximum
1067: tolerable probability(−25%). In addition, the delay with respect
1068: to soft deadlines, the fulﬁllment of which is not mandatory,
1069: is low (approximately 2.7 days), with a percentage of delayed
1070: activities of 14% with respect to the total number of processed
1071: activities within the 30 runs (2498). Regarding the RH steps,
1072: within the transition between two rolling frames, the number of
1073: non-executed activities that are postponed to the next RH frame
1074: is on average 0.89, while the infeasible solutions after an RH
1075: transition are 1.21. However, the infeasibility is automatically
1076: overcome by the MATHeuristic approach by varying the subset
1077: variables in the following MATHeuristic iteration, guaranteeing
1078: the feasibility of each RH step.
1079: VII. C ONCLUSION
1080: This article described a rolling-horizon approach for
1081: risk-based maintenance planning in the rail sector. The
1082: proposed methodology was proven to be a suitable tool to
1083: manage the maintenance activities of a large set of assets while
1084: dealing with uncertainty. In particular, the stochastic aspect of
1085: the rail deformation process was considered, starting from the
1086: degradation model deﬁned for a speciﬁc kind of asset, to evaluate
1087: the intervention deadlines that guarantee the desired low failure
1088: risk. The proposed approach is suitable for any other degradation
1089: model capable of providing an evaluation of the fault probability
1090: (or probability that the threshold is exceeded). This study
1091: aimed to advance the shift from a traditional preventive cyclical
1092: approach toward predictive strategies for maintenance planning,
1093: overcoming the static aspect of long-term decision-making by
1094: reﬁning the ofﬂine solution in case of receipt of updated informa-
1095: tion from the ﬁeld or unexpected events. The results of the case
1096: study pointed out the capability of the approach to react to exe-
1097: cution delays or priority changes, achieving good performance
1098: with respect to the basic top-to-end approach often applied in the
1099: maintenance of geographically distributed assets, which consists
1100: of the execution of rail maintenance according to the position of
1101: the rail stretches. Therefore, the proposed approach represents
1102: a useful decision-support system for short-term maintenance
1103: planning, introducing into maintenance decision support
1104: aspects that until now have been managed manually by human
1105: operators. Further studies will take into account the interaction
1106: with decision-support tools for long-term planning that can plan
1107: in advance possible service unavailability if the train-free time
1108: intervals are not long enough; future research will also consider
1109: possible penalties or extra costs for the infrastructure manager
1110: or the maintenance service provider if changes must be made
1111: to the previously deﬁned long-term schedule.

   8: A rolling horizon model for efficient load planning of intermodal trains 
   9: Abstract 
  10: With increasing efforts to make transportation sustainable, many big countries have started 
  11: expanding rail infrastructure to increase the double-stacking of containers, which doubles the 
  12: utilization of trains. However, double-stacking containers on wagons give rise to additional 
  13: operational and safety constraints which must be considered during the load planning of trains 
  14: at each terminal when containers from the storage yard are selected and assigned to loading 
  15: positions on wagons. Due to the complexity of the load planning problem and the limited time 
  16: available to generate a load plan, major train operators in India optimize the loading of only 
  17: one train at a time. This myopic planning negatively affects the utilization of future trains 
  18: undermining the benefits of double-stacking. In this paper, we first formulate a model for 
  19: simultaneous load planning of multiple trains and prove that the problem is NP-complete. Then, 
  20: we propose two new two-stage optimization approaches that first guarantee optimal utilization 
  21: of multiple trains and then improve the solution to maximize profit depending on the available 
  22: computation time for load planning. Experiments are conducted on real-life load planning 
  23: instances and the results show that the proposed approach outperforms the existing approach 
  24: to achieve better utilization and higher profit. 
  25: Keywords: Container train load planning, Double-stack container trains, Indian Railways, 
  26: Intermodal transport, Optimization 
  27: 1. Introduction 
  28: Intermodal containers are widely used to unitize cargo and enable the seamless transport of 
  29: cargo as standard units (containers) across multiple modes. Global container traffic, measured 
  30: in terms of TEUs (Twenty-foot equivalent units), has increased from 541 million in 2010 to 
  31: 798 million in 2020 [1]. Indian Railways (IR) is the fourth-largest rail network in the world in

  37: 2
  38: terms of route-kilometers [2]. It is also the fourth largest in the world in terms of freight carried 
  39: in tonne-kilometers [3]. In IR, the export-import container volume has increased from 23.29 
  40: million tonnes carried in 2009 to 50.55 million tonnes carried in 2021 [4], [5]. 
  41: Double-stack container trains are gaining more importance with the growing container traffic 
  42: and environmental concerns. These trains double wagon utilization and reduce transportation 
  43: costs, transit time, and CO 2 emissions per container. Although double-stack trains cannot be 
  44: operated in Europe due to a lower vertical clearance along the railway lines, many countries 
  45: such as Australia, Brazil, China, India, and the USA have developed the infrastructure and are 
  46: increasing the operation of these trains. IR invested about INR 800 billion to develop a 
  47: dedicated freight corridor capable of handling longer, heavier double-stack trains [6]. IR has 
  48: set a target to increase the container railway freight share from 21% in 2018 to 43% by 2031 
  49: [7]. Double-stack container trains will play a significant role in achieving this target. These 
  50: trains will not only carry more containers per train but will also reduce the dwell time of 
  51: containers at the terminal. 
  52: Container trains must be fully loaded to engender all the benefits of double-stacking. However, 
  53: when containers are double-stacked on wagons, several additional operational constraints must 
  54: be satisfied to ensure safe transit. Therefore, a container train load planning problem (CTLP) 
  55: is solved to select and assign containers to wagons. The input for CTLP is a set of containers 
  56: from the storage yard chosen by the terminal manager for loading on the next train. In case of 
  57: a large number of containers waiting in the storage yard, the terminal manager decides on a 
  58: cut-off time to shortlist the oldest containers, typically about twice the train capacity. CTLP 
  59: then selects containers from the input and assigns these to feasible loading positions on wagons 
  60: to maximize train utilization. The output of CTLP is a load plan which contains the details of 
  61: selected containers and their wagon loading positions.

  68: The IR infrastructure used by single-stack or double-stack trains is the same. Only the variable 
  69: cost incurred by IR increases for operating double-stack trains. Due to the lower marginal cost 
  70: of double-stacking and to better compete with road transport, IR provides a discount on the 
  71: containers loaded in the upper-stack [8]. The rail haulage cost (RHC) of a container is 
  72: proportional to its size (20-ft or 40-ft) and weight, which implies that a heavier container in the 
  73: upper stack will result in a larger discount. Therefore, train operators in India solve CTLP for 
  74: a more generic objective of maximizing profit, which also infers maximizing utilization of the 
  75: train because each loaded container has a profit associated with its haulage. 
  76: CTLP is an operational level problem. The train operators get about 15 to 30 minutes to 
  77: generate a load plan before train loading begins. Due to the time constraint, train operators in 
  78: India always optimize one train at a time [9]. However, the selection of containers for the 
  79: present train can negatively affect the utilization of future trains. To better match the containers 
  80: to loading positions on wagons in order to improve trains' utilization and profit, it is important 
  81: to optimize the load plan of multiple trains simultaneously. Hence, in this paper we focus on 
  82: the simultaneous load planning of multiple trains to maximize trains' utilization and profit. In 
  83: the literature, experiments by [9] show that maximizing profit for just one train is time 
  84: consuming and, in this paper, we prove that CTLP is NP-complete. Hence, we propose two 
  85: new two-stage solution approaches to effectively trade-off between computation time and 
  86: solution quality. 
  87: The paper is organized as follows. The literature on CTLP is discussed in Section 2. In Section 
  88: 3, CTLP is described in more detail, and its mathematical model is presented. Complexity proof 
  89: of the model is also derived in Section 3. Two new two-stage optimization approaches are 
  90: proposed in Section 4. In Section 5, the CTLP model and its solution approaches are validated 
  91: through various instances generated using real-life container train load plans. In Section 6, a

 100: 2. Intermodal operations and literature review 
 101: Containers are transported over long distances via ships, trains, and trucks. Each transportation 
 102: mode is typically managed by a different operator, such as a shipping line, a container train 
 103: operator, or a drayage operator. To facilitate an efficient transfer of containers between these 
 104: modes, terminal and port operators provide the requisite infrastructure and ancillary services. 
 105: Fig. 1: Intermodal freight operations and associated decision-making problems
 106: Fig. 1 summarizes a typical import process for the containers. Containers arriving on a ship at 
 107: a port are unloaded using cranes and transported to and stored in the storage yard. When a train 
 108: needs to be loaded, containers are retrieved from the storage yard using cranes and placed on 
 109: the trucks. These trucks then move the containers to the rail-side of the terminal near the 
 110: wagons assigned to the containers. Again, cranes are employed to pick up the containers from 
 111: the trucks and load these onto the wagons. The train then departs to its destination, where the 
 112: containers are unloaded and stored in the storage yard until the receiver of the containers sends 
 113: trucks to pick up the containers.

 120: The container train operator is responsible for planning train formation, routing, scheduling, 
 121: and loading, as mentioned in Fig. 1. A comprehensive review of rail yard operations is 
 122: presented by [10], and train routing, scheduling, and shunting problems are discussed by [11] 
 123: and [12]. CTLP is a complex planning problem, and hence, the problems of railroad blocking, 
 124: train routing and scheduling, and container routing are not considered in this paper. 
 125: After CTLP is solved, the generated load plan is shared with the container terminal operator. 
 126: The terminal operator is responsible for locating the containers from the load plan in the storage 
 127: yard, planning container retrieval operations, train loading and unloading operations, cranes 
 128: and trucks scheduling and routing, and storage space allocation of containers, as shown in Fig. 
 129: 1. An overview of container terminal operations and accompanying planning problems is 
 130: provided by [13], [14], and [15]. 
 131: Terminal operations planning problems, such as container retrieval problem and yard crane 
 132: scheduling problem are NP-hard, as shown by [16] and [17]. Moreover, we proved that CTLP 
 133: for double-stack trains is NP-complete. As both the terminal operations planning problems and 
 134: CTLP for double-stack trains are complex, terminal operations planning problems are solved 
 135: separately after CTLP. This is because combining the complex terminal operations and load 
 136: planning decisions for double-stack trains will make the combined problem intractable. 
 137: Further, it is more important to solve CTLP optimally than the terminal operations planning 
 138: problems because the savings from loading just one additional container can be up to INR 
 139: 50,000. This saving is many times the savings from minimizing crane movements while 
 140: retrieving containers from the storage yard and loading these on wagons of a train [18]. 
 141: Therefore, in this paper, we have focused only on CTLP for simultaneously planning multiple 
 142: trains.

 149: Few papers have worked on terminal operations planning for double-stack trains. A new 
 150: synchronous container handling scheme consisting of an automatic guided vehicle with a 
 151: loading and discharge function and a new special flat wagon is presented by [19]. The authors 
 152: conducted a cost-benefit analysis to show that the proposed container handling scheme reduces 
 153: the handling time and operating cost of double-stack trains compared to the traditional handling 
 154: scheme. To improve terminal operations planning, [20] exploited the multiple optimal 
 155: solutions of the CTLP model. The authors considered a given load plan for a double-stack train 
 156: and developed heuristics to modify it, while satisfying CTLP model constraints and without 
 157: changing the optimal utilization, to minimize total cranes' handling time. This time constitutes 
 158: total container retrieval and relocation time in the yard and loading and rehandling time on the 
 159: rail-side of the terminal. 
 160: CTLP for single-stack trains is a relatively simpler problem, and hence its literature considers 
 161: terminal operations planning decisions along with train load planning decisions [21]. A CTLP 
 162: model was formulated and solved by [22] to minimize train length, container rehandling time, 
 163: movement time, and time taken to change the wagon loading pattern. A CTLP model 
 164: considering different container lengths and their weight restrictions on wagons was presented 
 165: by [23]. The objectives of maximizing utilization and minimizing the time taken to change the 
 166: wagon loading pattern and transportation cost for loading were considered. A CTLP model to 
 167: maximize utilization and minimize unproductive operations at the terminal was formulated by 
 168: [24]. The authors proposed three solution approaches and compared them for their suitability 
 169: for practical implementation. A CTLP model to maximize the total priority of loaded containers 
 170: and minimize container rehandling in the yard was proposed and solved by [25]. 
 171: As the focus of this paper is to solve CTLP for double-stack trains, from now on, CTLP refers 
 172: to the CTLP for double-stack container trains. One of the first works to solve CTLP developed 
 173: container-oriented and location-oriented automatic suggestion heuristics to load containers on

 186: In the US, the train operators assign only one destination per track. This results in lower 
 187: utilization of railcars on a track if sufficient demand for that destination is not available. Lower 
 188: utilization can also result if the available containers violate operational constraints. A model 
 189: specific to US operations was presented by [28] to assign containers to railcars and railcars to 
 190: destinations while allowing the assignment of railcars on a track to multiple destinations, 
 191: increasing the utilization of railcars. Later, to reduce the computation time of solving the model, 
 192: [29] proposed a three-stage solution approach that tightens the lower and upper bounds. 
 193: However, the blocking and shunting practices in the US are not permitted in India. 
 194: To improve the aerodynamic efficiency of the trains, [30] formulated a CTLP model to 
 195: minimize the total adjusted gap length between containers and solved the model in CPLEX. 
 196: Later, the model was extended to include multiple trains and solved using a rolling horizon 
 197: approach [31]. However, [9] argued that the benefits from minimizing aerodynamic resistance 
 198: would be substantial only if there is a significant variation in the container and wagon lengths 
 199: and if train speed is very high. It is noteworthy that over 97% of container rail traffic in India 
 200: consists of 20-ft and 40-ft containers.

 224: The major contributions of this paper are as follows. First, we discuss the effects of restricting 
 225: the planning horizon when generating the load plan. We also highlight the shortcoming of the 
 226: approach present in the literature as well as used in practice to counter these effects. Second, 
 227: for the first time in the literature, we prove the computational complexity of CTLP. Third, we 
 228: present the CTLP model for multiple trains and provide two alternative two-stage optimization-
 229: based solution approaches. Fourth, we perform detailed computational experiments for the 
 230: proposed solution approaches under different scenarios generated using real-life container train 
 231: load plan data from a major train operator in India. From the experiments we show that for two 
 232: trains solving CTLP to maximize utilization is much less computationally challenging than 
 233: solving CTLP to maximize profit. We analyze the financial benefits and computational issues

 242: 3. Container train load planning model
 243: 3.1. Problem formulation
 244: This section discusses a mathematical model of CTLP for planning multiple trains 
 245: simultaneously. The input set of containers consists of 20-ft (1 TEU) and 40-ft (2 TEUs) 
 246: containers, referred to as the 20s and 40s. ISO containers of height 8'6" and 9'6" are 
 247: considered. 
 248: IR allows four feasible loading patterns for loading containers on wagons, as shown in Fig. 
 249: 2, and each wagon can accommodate at most four TEUs. A wagon loaded in pattern 1 can 
 250: accommodate two 20s in the lower-stack and one 40 in the upper-stack. The height of the 
 251: 20s should be the same to balance the upper-stack container. Pattern 2 indicates a wagon 
 252: loaded with a 40 in the lower and the upper-stack. Patterns 3 and 4 are single-stacked 
 253: wagons loaded with two 20s and one 40, respectively. 
 254: Fig. 2: Feasible loading patterns of the 20s and 40s on wagons
 255: Other possible patterns, such as loading a 40 in the lower-stack and two 20s in the upper-
 256: stack, and loading four 20s on a wagon, are not feasible. This infeasibility is because a 40 
 257: in the lower-stack does not have corner castings at its center to secure the 20s above it. 
 258: Also, loading four 20s on a wagon is prohibited by IR due to safety reasons. Moreover, for 
 259: safety, empty wagons and double-stack wagons cannot coexist on a train. Hence, empty 
 260: wagons are not considered in the CTLP model.

 360: The objective function for maximizing train utilization: 
 361: Train utilization is modelled as the maximization of total TEUs loaded on the trains, as 
 362: shown by equation (13). 
 363: The objective function for maximizing profit: 
 364: Rail haulage cost (RHC) is a major operating cost that a train operator pays to IR for using 
 365: the rail infrastructure, locomotives, and crew to operate the trains. RHC depends upon 
 366: container characteristics such as its length, weight, and wagon loading position. Profit for 
 367: the train operator is obtained by subtracting the RHC of a container from the revenue 
 368: received from the consignor for transporting the container. Therefore, after maximizing 
 369: utilization, the second important objective of the train operator is to maximize the total 
 370: profit or minimize the total RHC. 
 371: As IR provides a 50% discount on the containers loaded in the upper-stack [8] and RHC 
 372: increases with container weight, the train operator aims to load heavier containers in the 
 373: upper-stack positions. The concept of rearranging containers to maximize profit while 
 374: loading the same set of containers on the train is referred to as position arbitrage. Position 
 375: arbitrage gain refers to the additional profit gained by the train operator by exchanging a 
 376: lighter container in the upper-stack with a heavier container in the lower-stack of a train 
 377: [32].

 475: Another advantage of simultaneously planning multiple trains is that it provides an 
 476: opportunity to further reduce the total RHC of the trains by rearranging containers across 
 477: trains. That is, a lighter container in the upper-stack of one train can be exchanged with a 
 478: heavier container in the lower-stack of another train, thereby decreasing the total RHC of 
 479: the trains. Analogous to position arbitrage, this concept is referred to as time arbitrage as 
 480: it involves multiple trains. Time arbitrage gain is the RHC saved by exchanging suitable 
 481: containers across trains.

 506: From the above discussion, it is clear that simultaneously planning multiple trains increases 
 507: trains' utilization and savings in RHC. However, CTLP is a complex problem where the 
 508: computation time increases exponentially with the size of the input. In many train load 
 509: planning instances, CTLP with OF2a (Eq. 16) as the objective function cannot be solved 
 510: optimally, even for two trains of 40-45 wagons each (typical train size in India) in two to 
 511: three hours. The following section discusses the computational complexity of the basic 
 512: CTLP. 
 513: 3.2. Complexity proof of CTLP 
 514: The complexity proof is shown for the basic CTLP model, i.e., the additional constraints, 
 515: such as equations 9-12, are not considered here. Also, the proof is presented considering 
 516: the load planning of only one train. We show that CTLP is NP-complete in both cases when 
 517: either utilization or profit is maximized. That is, CTLP is NP-complete whether the profit 
 518: depends on the container loading position on the wagon or not. To prove NP-completeness, 
 519: we define the decision version of CTLP as follows:

 605: We proved that CTLP is NP-complete when the profit does not depend on the position of 
 606: containers on the wagons. However, it is easy to extend that CTLP remains NP-complete 
 607: if the profit depends on the position. To explain this, suppose a polynomial-time algorithm 
 608: exists for CTLP when the profit depends on the position. Then, we can use this algorithm 
 609: to solve CTLP instances in polynomial-time when the profit does not depend on the 
 610: position by assigning equal profit to all positions. This will contradict our assumption that 
 611: P ≠  NP. In the next section, we propose two new solution approaches to address the trade-
 612: off between computation time and solution quality effectively.

 619: 4. Solution approaches 
 620: Two objectives of maximizing utilization OF1a (Eq. 15) and profit OF2a (Eq. 16) are 
 621: defined for the CTLP model in Section 3. The objectives OF1a and OF2a are non-
 622: conflicting. That is, the optimal solution of OF2a will always be an optimal solution of 
 623: OF1a, although vice-versa is not true. Therefore, it should be sufficient to optimize OF2a 
 624: to optimize both OF1a and OF2a. However, from the experiments discussed in Section 5.1, 
 625: we know that it is much more challenging computationally to solve CTLP with OF2a than 
 626: to solve CTLP with OF1a for two trains within an acceptable time limit. If an optimal 
 627: solution of OF2a is not obtained, then even OF1a, a more important objective, will also be 
 628: compromised. In practice, the train operators would always want to ensure optimal 
 629: utilization of the trains because it is the most important factor in generating revenue. We 
 630: know that the CTLP model with OF1a is symmetric due to identical wagon payload 
 631: capacities and several feasible container loading arrangements on wagons, which results in 
 632: multiple optima. Therefore, after maximizing utilization, the train operators will then focus 
 633: on maximizing total profit further to the extent possible. Hence, we present two two-stage 
 634: optimization approaches, which first guarantee optimal trains' utilization and then use the 
 635: remaining computation time to maximize profit. 
 636: 4.1. Two-stage optimization approach-I

 638: to plan two trains simultaneously.

 755: Stage-1 of TSO-II is the same as that of TSO-I. That is, the CTLP model with OF1a (Eq.

 757: the optimal solution from Stage-1 are denoted by 𝕆∗ and 𝕊∗, respectively. 
 758: For Stage-2, with the input of sets 𝐼1 and 𝐼2, the CTLP model with OF2a as the objective 
 759: function for 𝑡 = 1 is considered to maximize profit only for the first train. Equation (17) is 
 760: added as a constraint, and the model is solved by warm-starting it with 𝕊∗. The output load 
 761: plan for train 𝑡 = 1 from Stage-2, denoted by 𝕃1∗
 762: , is generated to maximize profit. As 
 763: constraint (17) ensures that every feasible solution from Stage-2 is an optimal solution of

 771: for the first train can be maximized within the practical time limits without compromising 
 772: the utilization of future trains. 
 773: To implement the TSO-II approach, a rolling horizon framework is employed. In this 
 774: framework, the model is solved for a longer planning horizon (two trains), and then a part 
 775: of the solution is implemented for a shorter horizon called the control horizon (one train). 
 776: As time progresses, new and uncertain information is realized, and the input sets 𝐼𝑙, 𝐾𝑡, and 
 777: 𝐺 
 778: 𝑘𝑡 are updated at the end of the control horizon. The model is then solved again for the 
 779: next planning horizon. The framework is illustrated in Fig. 6.

 795: For clarity of presentation, we refer to the CTLP model with OF1a as CTLP-I and OF2a as 
 796: CTLP-II, respectively. The approach of solving CTLP-I and CTLP-II for simultaneously 
 797: planning multiple trains is called simultaneous optimization-I (SO-I) and simultaneous 
 798: optimization-II (SO-II), respectively. The single-stage optimization (SSO) approach solves 
 799: CTLP-II for one train at a time and is the state-of-the-art approach currently used by train 
 800: operators. In SSO, CTLP-II is solved for the first train with an input of 𝐼𝑙. The remaining 
 801: containers in 𝐼𝑙, which are not loaded on the first train, denoted by ℐ1
 802: 𝑙 , are then used as input 
 803: to solve CTLP-II again for the second train. All the solution approaches are summarized in 
 804: Fig. 5. 
 805: The next section demonstrates detailed numerical experiments conducted to validate the 
 806: proposed solution approaches for the CTLP model. Each subsection compares different 
 807: solution approaches and quantifies the benefits of the approaches based on the obtained 
 808: train utilization and RHC savings.

 815: 5. Numerical Experiments
 816: To assess the performance of different solution approaches for the CTLP model, we 
 817: collected the data of actual container train load plans from two major train operators in 
 818: India. We obtained the data for six origin-destination (OD) pairs on which double-stack 
 819: container trains are operated. The origin terminal of these OD pairs is rake-deficit, i.e., the 
 820: number of containers to be transported is higher than the wagons available for transport. 
 821: Therefore, it is crucial to achieve optimal train utilization at these terminals. Rake-surplus 
 822: terminals have a higher number of wagons than containers to transport. Therefore, many 
 823: wagons on the departing train are not double-stacked at the rake-surplus terminal, making 
 824: it relatively easier to solve CTLP. However, at the same time, it becomes essential to use 
 825: the CTLP model for load planning so as to select heavier upper-stack containers that 
 826: maximize profit. 
 827: The container details consist of the container's weight, height, and length. The weight of 
 828: 20s and 40s can vary between 2.5-tonne (empty) to 33-tonne and 4-tonne (empty) to 33-
 829: tonne, respectively. The train details consist of wagon composition and payload capacity. 
 830: In IR, most trains are direct trains with no intermediate handling. Our solution approach 
 831: works well for direct trains as it results in more arbitrage gain opportunities. A typical train 
 832: consists of 40 to 45 wagons. For the experiments, the trains of 40 wagons each are 
 833: considered to perform a detailed analysis within reasonable computation times. The value

 900: The scenarios are generated to highlight the effect of different solution approaches for the 
 901: CTLP model on the computation time, optimality gap, train utilization, and RHC savings. 
 902: The experiments are performed using CPLEX v20.1.0 optimization software on a 16-core 
 903: Intel Xeon processor with 32 GB RAM. 
 904: The input data has its origin terminal as a rake-deficit terminal. However, if we consider 
 905: the number of containers in 𝐼𝑙 to be more than the train's loading capacity, then each 
 906: objective function and solution approach can select a different set of containers to be loaded 
 907: on the first train as well as the second train due to multiple optimal solutions. If the set of 
 908: loaded containers changes, the RHC savings from different solution approaches cannot be 
 909: compared. Therefore, we perform the experiments for the worst-case scenario where the 
 910: number of containers in 𝐼𝑙 is equal to the train's loading capacity. Note that if the number 
 911: of containers in 𝐼𝑙 is above the train's capacity, the CTLP model can explore more arbitrage 
 912: gain possibilities which typically results in a decrease in computational time. 
 913: Section 5.A compares the performance of SO-I and SO-II to quantify the arbitrage gain that 
 914: can be obtained while loading the same set of containers on the trains. It also highlights the 
 915: challenges associated with solving SO-II. Section 5.B compares the performance of SO-II 
 916: and TSO-I. Section 5.C compares the performance of SSO, SO-II, and TSO-II. SSO is the 
 917: state-of-the-art approach currently used by train operators. 
 918: All the train instances of Sections 5.A-5.C consider the planning of two trains of 40 wagons 
 919: each. These two trains are scheduled consecutively on the same OD route. The number of 
 920: containers in the input set is equal to the total train's loading capacity of 320 TEUs. For 
 921: comparison, no container is added after the first train is loaded.

 932: to 5, respectively. The instances are sorted in increasing order of the payload capacity, and 
 933: for each payload capacity, the instances are again sorted in increasing order of the number 
 934: of 40s. Columns 6 and 7 show the total optimal RHC of trains 𝑇1 and 𝑇2 obtained from SO-
 935: II and SO-I, respectively. Column 8 shows the savings in RHC due to arbitrage gain. 
 936: For the purpose of comparing different solution approaches, optimal utilization, and 
 937: optimal profit are required. However, we found that SO-II typically takes a long

 939: desired time limit of about 15 minutes. Therefore, for even comparison, the computation

1023: 5.2. Experiments to compare SO-II and TSO-I 
1024: The first and second stages of TSO-I are equivalent to SO-I and SO-II, respectively. The 
1025: benefit of using TSO-I over SO-II is that it allows the train operator to maximize profit 
1026: after optimizing utilization. Optimal utilization of the trains can typically be achieved 
1027: within the first ten minutes (column 10 of Table 1). Hence, after ensuring optimal 
1028: utilization, the train operator can use the available computation time to leverage arbitrage 
1029: gains and maximize profit. 
1030: 5.3. Experiments to compare SSO, SO-II, and TSO-II

1033: approaches is compared in terms of utilization and savings in RHC. A computation time of 
1034: two hours and an optimality gap of 0.2% is allowed for each instance, which enables the 
1035: comparison of optimal utilization and RHC savings.

1294: 6. Execution of load plans 
1295: When multiple trains are planned together, as is the case in TSO-II, some containers that 
1296: arrived earlier are assigned to trains that depart late. This delay can result in customer 
1297: grievances which affect the service quality provided by the train operators. Therefore, the 
1298: train operators prefer to load the containers on a first-come-first-serve basis (FCFS) in order 
1299: to provide timely service to their customers and minimize customer grievances. This FCFS 
1300: requirement also explains that simultaneous optimization of three or more trains cannot be 
1301: implemented, even if we can find an optimal solution for three trains.

1308: Although it is not possible to strictly follow FCFS when planning double-stack trains due 
1309: to operational and safety constraints, it is essential to reduce FCFS violations. To enable 
1310: train operators to improve their compliance with FCFS rules, an algorithm, Algorithm-3, is 
1311: proposed. Algorithm-3 reassign containers to wagons based on their arrival time at the 
1312: terminal, while keeping the load plans of trains 𝑇1 and 𝑇2 optimal. The algorithm is 
1313: developed for the general case where the input set of containers for the CTLP model 𝐼𝑙 is 
1314: more than the total loading capacity of trains 𝑇1 and 𝑇2. The algorithm takes the load plans

1405: 7. Conclusions
1406: The purpose of introducing double-stack trains is to handle the growing container traffic 
1407: efficiently. Therefore, it is crucial to maximize train utilization by simultaneously planning 
1408: multiple trains because even one empty slot on a train can cost up to INR 50,000. This cost 
1409: is many times more than the savings from optimizing any of the secondary objectives of 
1410: load planning. 
1411: This paper presents a CTLP model with the objectives of maximizing utilization and profit 
1412: for multiple trains. We prove that the CTLP model is NP-complete and cannot be solved in 
1413: practical time limits for multiple trains. To effectively trade-off between the solution 
1414: quality and computation time, we propose two two-stage optimization approaches (TSO-I 
1415: and TSO-II). These approaches guarantee optimal utilization of the trains in about five to 
1416: ten minutes and then use the remaining time to optimize the profit further. 
1417: We conduct extensive experiments on real-life train load plans to analyze and compare the 
1418: performance of different solution approaches under different scenarios. The results indicate 
1419: that TSO-II performs better than other approaches in terms of achieved utilization, RHC 
1420: This preprint research paper has not been peer reviewed. Electronic copy available at: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4891256
1421: Preprint not peer reviewed
1422: 
1423: ## --- PAGE 41 ---
1424: 
1425: 41
1426: savings, and computation time taken to generate the load plans. The results also show that 
1427: by planning multiple trains simultaneously, time arbitrage gains can also be exploited along 
1428: with additional position arbitrage gains. 
1429: The TSO-II approach, in most instances, is able to obtain a near-optimal solution for train 
1430: 𝑇1. At high-traffic terminals, TSO-II can generate solutions with optimal utilization of 
1431: multiple trains and maximize profit for the first train within a reasonable optimality gap. 
1432: At low-traffic terminals, more time is available for TSO-II to solve the CTLP model 
1433: optimally. 
1434: Heuristics, commonly used for large-scale optimization, are not proposed in this paper as, 
1435: unlike TSO-II, they may not guarantee optimal train utilization. In the future, efficient 
1436: algorithms can be developed based on the TSO-II approach, i.e., first maximizing the train 
1437: utilization and then applying heuristics to maximize the profit further. 
1438: Moreover, in the future, a model can be developed to account for simultaneous train loading 
1439: and unloading operations at the terminal. A more complex hub and spoke network with 
1440: multiple OD pairs can also be considered when planning multiple trains. Integrating 
1441: terminal operations planning with load planning decisions is also a potential future research 
1442: direction.
